one_liner: Small C++ optimal-parse LZ4 encoder: standard .lz4 output about 0.2-0.9% smaller than lz4 -9/-12, but slower to compress.
what_it_does: smallz4 compresses data into the standard LZ4 frame format (or the legacy format with -l) using optimal parsing, so any LZ4 decoder can read the output. The library is one header-only class: smallz4::lz4(getBytes, sendBytes, maxChainLength, dictionary, useLegacyFormat, userPtr) pulls input and pushes output through C function-pointer callbacks. It has no in-memory buffer API and no decompressor in the header; smallz4cat.c is a separate tiny C99 streaming decoder.
how_it_is_fast: It is not faster than the baseline; the gain is output size. Level 9 walks the full hash chain inside LZ4's 64 KB window for every position (findLongestMatch), then runs a backward dynamic-programming pass (estimateCosts) that picks, for each position, the match length or literal that minimises encoded bytes, including the extra length bytes at 15 and 15+255n. Levels 1-3 are greedy and 4-6 lazy with chain lengths 1-6, which skip the DP-heavy search.
when_to_use: Compress-once, decompress-many LZ4 assets (firmware images, game data, embedded payloads) where every byte counts and encode time is irrelevant
When the decoder is fixed to the LZ4 format and cannot be swapped for zstd or LZSA
Vendoring a tiny, dependency-free MIT encoder (one header, about 800 lines) plus a few-hundred-line C decoder for small or static binaries
Preset-dictionary LZ4 compression (-D) where both sides share the last 64 KB of a dictionary file
when_not_to_use: Any throughput-sensitive compression: snippet figures put level 9 at 224-262 s for enwik9 versus 33 s for lz4 r128 -9 and 144 s for lz4 1.8.2 -12
If you already use modern lz4 -12: snippet data show lz4 1.8.2 -12 --no-frame-crc -BD at 371,680,440 bytes versus smallz4 1.1 at 371,680,428, a 12-byte difference on 1 GB

Inputs with long repeats at a period above 1 byte (for example a short pattern or a small record repeated for megabytes) at levels 7-9: from reading the code, every position gets a match running to the block end and both the match finder and estimateCosts scan that length, so time grows roughly quadratically per 4 MB block (not measured); only single-byte runs are short-cut via MaxSameLetter
Large or memory-tight inputs: per 4 MB block it allocates a 16-byte Match per input byte plus a 4-byte cost per byte and an 8 MB hash table, roughly 90 MB peak (from the code's vector sizes)
Projects needing a maintained library with an in-memory API, multithreading or block-independent output

integration.min_toolchain: C++98-style code built with g++ -O2 in the Makefile (no -std set); smallz4cat needs C99. The Makefile says it was only tested on the author's Linux system.
integration.platforms: any in principle; the encoder reads 4 bytes through uint32_t* casts at arbitrary offsets, so it relies on unaligned loads being tolerated (x86-64, ARMv8); strict-alignment targets are not documented
integration.thread_safety: not documented; each lz4() call builds its own compressor object with no global state, so concurrent calls on separate streams look safe from the code
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: output is standard LZ4 frame or legacy format readable by lz4 and liblz4, but the encoder API is a callback interface, not LZ4_compress_HC() or the LZ4F API

gotchas: Frames are written with linked blocks (block-independence flag off), 4 MB max block size and no content or block checksum, so output cannot be decoded block-by-block in parallel and corruption is not detected; smallz4cat also reads and ignores any checksums in other files.
With a dictionary (-D) the frame carries no dictionary ID, so decoders must be handed the same dictionary out of band (lz4 -D or smallz4cat -D).

smallz4cat bugs from reading smallz4cat.c (not tested): with -D it opens argv[1] instead of the file argument, so 'smallz4cat -D dict file.lz4' tries to open '-D'; one-character file names are ignored; a legacy-format file whose size is an exact multiple of 8 MiB ends with 'ERROR: out of data' and exit code 1 after writing the full output; offsets reaching before the stream start copy uninitialised stack bytes from its 64 KB history buffer.

The encoder reads 4 bytes through *(uint32_t*) casts (unaligned type-punning, undefined behaviour in C++ though fine on x86 and ARMv8), and the CLI never checks fwrite results or sets binary mode on stdin/stdout, so Windows pipes are text mode.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick smallz4 over lz4 -12 only for the last few hundred bytes per gigabyte and a dependency-free single header; pick lz4ultra or blz4 for the same optimal-LZ4 goal with faster encoders or decode-speed tuning (lz4ultra's enwik9 size of 371,680,323 bytes is within 5 bytes of smallz4's), and plain LZ4 HC when compression speed matters at all.
verified_claims_summary: First-party enwik9 (1 GiB English Wikipedia) numbers known only from WebSearch snippets of the author's egress-blocked page and encode.su: smallz4 0.5 -9 371,681,075 bytes in 224 s versus lz4 r128 -9 374,905,570 bytes (0.86% smaller) and lz4 -12 371,681,832 bytes in 144 s; smallz4 1.5 -9 371,680,328 bytes versus lz4 1.9.2 -12 372,443,347 bytes (0.2% smaller). Machine, compiler and flags are not stated, and decode speed is that of whichever LZ4 decoder you use.
status_note: Abandoned (GitHub mirror last commit 2020-04-13, version string 1.5, 3 issues, no pull requests; the author's site is the stated main repository) but MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor.
